title: The simplex criterion for sharp simplicial maps
statement:
Use small simplicial sets, standard simplices $\Delta^n$, monomorphisms and weak homotopy equivalences of [lem-coef-kan-quillen-model-right-proper-core], and sharp maps and homotopy-cartesian squares of [lem-coef-sharp-pullback-calculus]. Let $p:E\to B$ be any map of small simplicial sets. The following are equivalent:
(i) $p$ is sharp.
(ii) For every $n\geq0$ and every simplicial map $\sigma:\Delta^n\to B$, the strict pullback square $E\times_B\Delta^n\to E$ over $\Delta^n\to B$ is homotopy cartesian.
(iii) For every $m,n\geq0$, every simplicial map $\delta:\Delta^m\to\Delta^n$, and every $\sigma:\Delta^n\to B$, the induced map $E\times_{B,\sigma\delta}\Delta^m\to E\times_{B,\sigma}\Delta^n$ is a weak homotopy equivalence.
No fibrancy hypothesis is imposed on $E$ or $B$.

source.place: Remark 4.2(1)-(3), printed p. 9, following Theorem 4.1; specialization to the topos of sets. Read online 2026-10-17. No Stacks tag states this simplicial homotopy criterion; archive WANTED.

proof.text: Write $W$ for the weak homotopy equivalences and $E_T=E\times_B T$ for a map $T\to B$. If (i) holds, the definition of sharpness says that every strict pullback square along every $T\to B$ is homotopy cartesian. Taking $T=\Delta^n$ proves (ii).

Every map $\delta:\Delta^m\to\Delta^n$ belongs to $W$. Indeed the realized simplices are closed disks, including a point in dimension zero. Each disk is nonempty and has a contraction to any chosen point $a$, given in convex disk coordinates by $(x,t)\mapsto(1-t)x+ta$. It therefore has one path component and trivial positive homotopy groups at every point. Any map between two such realizations induces the required bijection and isomorphisms. This argument requires neither simplex to be Kan.

source.place: Theorem 4.1(2) implies (4) and Remark 4.2, printed p. 9; explicit contractibility argument.

proof.text: Assume (ii). Factor $p:E\to B$ as a weak equivalence $E\to\widehat E$ followed by a Kan fibration $\widehat E\to B$. For $\sigma:\Delta^n\to B$, factor $\sigma$ as a weak equivalence $\Delta^n\to T_\sigma$ followed by a Kan fibration $T_\sigma\to B$. Write $P_\sigma=E\times_B\Delta^n$ and $Q_\sigma=\widehat E\times_B\Delta^n$. The fibrant replacements of the two legs over $B$ compute the homotopy pullback: by (ii), $P_\sigma\to\widehat E\times_B T_\sigma$ lies in $W$. Right properness makes $Q_\sigma\to\widehat E\times_B T_\sigma$ a weak equivalence, since it is the pullback of $\Delta^n\to T_\sigma$ along the Kan fibration $\widehat E\times_B T_\sigma\to T_\sigma$. Two-out-of-three gives the canonical comparison $P_\sigma\to Q_\sigma$ in $W$. For $\delta:\Delta^m\to\Delta^n$, the comparison $Q_{\sigma\delta}\to Q_\sigma$ is the pullback of $\delta$ along the Kan fibration $Q_\sigma\to\Delta^n$, so right properness and step 2 make it a weak equivalence. The commuting square with the two canonical maps $P\to Q$ and two-out-of-three give $P_{\sigma\delta}\to P_\sigma$ in $W$. No original object is assumed Kan; all fibrations used are over the indicated base. This is the over-$B$ fibrant-leg computation of Rezk Section 2.3.

source.place: Remark 4.2(2) implies (3), printed p. 9, expanded using the fibrant-replacement definition in Section 2.3.

proof.text: Assume (iii). We prove the local horn assertion used below by an induction that is uniform in the simplex dimension. Say that $q:F\to\Delta^r$ satisfies the local condition if $F\times_{\Delta^r}\Delta^s\to F$ belongs to $W$ for every simplex operator $\Delta^s\to\Delta^r$. For an inclusion $D\cong\Delta^d\hookrightarrow\Delta^r$ of a nonempty face, the restricted map $F_D\to D$ again satisfies the local condition: for $\eta:\Delta^s\to D$, both $F_{D,\eta}\to F$ and $F_D\to F$ are in $W$, hence $F_{D,\eta}\to F_D$ is in $W$ by two-out-of-three. The inductive claim is: for every $r$, every $q$ satisfying the local condition, every vertex $v$ of $\Delta^r$, and every nonempty collection $J$ of distinct codimension-one faces containing $v$, the inclusion $F\times_{\Delta^r}(\bigcup_{j\in J}D_j)\to F$ belongs to $W$. Induct on $|J|$, for all $r,q,v$ simultaneously. When $|J|=1$ this is exactly the local condition for its single face. There is no nonempty such collection in dimension zero.

source.place: Lemma 9.3 and Corollaries 6.5–6.6, printed pp. 12 and 20: explicit finite face-union induction, base and restriction condition.

proof.text: For the induction step in step 4, write $J=J'\amalg\{j\}$ with $J'$ nonempty, put $H'=\bigcup_{a\in J'}D_a$, and put $D=D_j$. Inside $D\cong\Delta^{r-1}$ the intersection $H'\cap D$ is the union of the $|J'|$ distinct codimension-one faces $D_a\cap D$, all containing $v$. Thus the induction hypothesis, applied first to $q$ and $J'$ and then to its restriction over $D$ and these intersections, gives $A:=F\times H'\to F$ and $C:=F\times(H'\cap D)\to F_D$ in $W$; all these products are over $\Delta^r$. Also $F_D\to F$ is in $W$ by the local condition, so $C\to F$ is in $W$. The inclusions $C\to A$ and $C\to F_D$ are monomorphisms. Degreewise the union is the pushout $A\amalg_C F_D=F\times_{\Delta^r}(H'\cup D)$: pairs in the intersection are identified once, and every pair in the union is in one of the two pieces. Apply the cited weak-equivalence gluing statement to the map of spans $(A\leftarrow C\to F_D)\to(F\leftarrow F\to F)$, where both maps of the second span are identities. The three component maps to $F$ are in $W$ and the required left legs $C\to A$ and $1_F$ are monomorphisms. It gives $A\amalg_C F_D\to F$ in $W$, completing the induction.

source.place: Lemma 9.3, printed p. 20: finite cofibrant face diagram; expansion of the induction behind Corollary 6.5 by the pushout gluing lemma.

proof.text: For any $\sigma:\Delta^n\to B$ take $F=E\times_B\Delta^n$ over $\Delta^n$. It satisfies the local condition by (iii) and associativity of strict pullbacks. For $n\geq1$ and $0\leq k\leq n$, the faces $D_j$ with $j\ne k$ are exactly the codimension-one faces containing vertex $k$, and their union is $\Lambda_k^n$. Steps 4–5 therefore show $E\times_B\Lambda_k^n\to E\times_B\Delta^n$ is in $W$. It is also a monomorphism, hence a trivial cofibration in the Kan–Quillen structure. In dimension one the horn is its single retained vertex, already the base case; no zero-dimensional horn is used.

source.place: Lemma 9.3, printed pp. 20–21, specialized to the topos of sets and a single simplex.

proof.text: We extend step 6 to trivial cofibrations over $B$. Strict pullback $p^*:\mathrm{sSet}_{/B}\to\mathrm{sSet}_{/E}$ preserves all small colimits by [lem-coef-sset-pullback-preserves-colimits]. It preserves monomorphisms because an injective map on the second coordinates gives an injective map on pairs. The Kan–Quillen cell description writes a trivial cofibration $i:A\hookrightarrow A\prime$ as an arrow retract of a transfinite horn-cell composite $j:C\to C\prime$. Write its section maps as $a:A\to C$, $b:A\prime\to C\prime$ and retractions as $r:C\to A$, $s:C\prime\to A\prime$, with $ja=bi$, $ir=sj$, $ra=1_A$, $sb=1_{A\prime}$. If $q:A\prime\to B$ is the given structure map, give $C\prime$ the map $qs$ and $C$ the map $qsj=qir$. Then $a,b,r,s$ lie over $B$: the equations for $a,b$ follow from $ra=1_A$, $sb=1_{A\prime}$, and those for $r,s$ follow from the definitions. Give all horn attachments and intermediate stages their composite maps through $C\prime$ to $B$. Hence this is a retract of a continuous horn-cell diagram in the slice, and pullback preserves its retract and every cell colimit.

source.place: Proposition 9.1(3) implies (1), printed pp. 19–20; distributive law Proposition 3.7, printed p. 6, proved degreewise here; Kan–Quillen horn generation replaces the Boolean-localization generation theorem.

proof.text: Each horn attachment in the pulled-back diagram of step 7 is a trivial cofibration by step 6, for its own structure map $\Delta^n\to B$. Put $T$ equal to the class of all Kan fibrations in $\mathrm{sSet}$. Trivial cofibrations have the left lifting property against $T$, by the model structure. Coproducts retain that property: a square on a coproduct restricts to a square on each summand; choose the lifts and combine them by the coproduct universal property. Pushouts and arrow retracts retain it by [lem-coef-lifting-class-closure], and continuous small transfinite composites retain it by [lem-coef-transfinite-left-lifting]. Thus $p^*i$ has the left lifting property against all Kan fibrations. To see explicitly that this implies a trivial cofibration, factor $p^*i$ as a trivial cofibration $c$ followed by a Kan fibration $t$. Lifting against $t$ gives $h$ with $th=1$ and $h(p^*i)=c$; the maps $(1,h)$ and $(1,t)$ exhibit $p^*i$ as an arrow retract of $c$. Cofibrations and weak equivalences are closed under retracts by the model axioms. Therefore $p^*i$ is a trivial cofibration and lies in $W$.

source.place: Proposition 9.1(3) implies (1), printed pp. 19–20; distributive law Proposition 3.7, printed p. 6, proved degreewise here; Kan–Quillen horn generation replaces the Boolean-localization generation theorem.

proof.text: Finally let $u:A\to A'$ be an arbitrary weak homotopy equivalence over $B$. Factor its underlying map as a trivial cofibration $i:A\to Z$ followed by a fibration $t:Z\to A'$, and give $Z$ the composite map to $B$. Two-out-of-three makes $t$ a trivial fibration. Steps 7–8 makes $p^*i$ a weak equivalence. The pullback $p^*t$ is a trivial fibration as well: a boundary-lifting problem for $p^*t$ projects to one for $t$; the resulting lift has the required map to $E$ because that coordinate is the prescribed bottom map, and the equality over $B$ follows from the bottom triangle. The boundary-lifting characterization in the cited model theorem, including the zero-dimensional boundary, therefore makes $p^*t$ a weak equivalence. Their composite $p^*u$ is in $W$. The weak-equivalence-preservation characterization of sharpness now gives (i). Together with steps 1 and 3 this proves all three conditions equivalent for arbitrary small $E$ and $B$.

source.place: Proposition 9.1, printed pp. 19–20, reduction from weak equivalences to trivial cofibrations; Proposition 2.7 and Remark 4.2.

proof_origin.place: Remark 4.2, Proposition 9.1 and Lemma 9.3 (printed pp. 9, 19–21), read online 2026-10-17; finite-face induction and slice-colimit argument expanded by NV. Archive absent from literature/: WANTED in report.md. Q58: checked the online source; extracted Proposition 3.7 as its own statement-only child, used existing lifting-class leaves, and used fibrant-leg replacements over B in step 3.
